channel.title: Shivam Negi: Writing
channel.description: Guides and book reviews on AI systems.

item.title: System 1, System 2: How to Give Your AI a Fast Path and a Slow Path
item.description: Why a production LLM system should run two paths, a fast default and a slow verified escalation, and how to build the router, the gate, and the evals that keep it honest.

item.title: How to Shrink a Transformer for CPU Serving Without Losing Your Mind (or Accuracy)
item.description: A field manual for distilling, pruning, and quantizing language models for CPU-only, latency-critical serving, and why most of the tricks fail before one works.

item.title: Why Your Voice Agent Feels Rude: Latency, Turn-Taking, and Barge-In
item.description: A systems view of real-time voice agents, why 800 ms feels broken, and how to engineer the pipeline, the turn-taking model, and the evals so conversations feel human.

item.title: How to Build a RAG System That Says "I Don't Know"
item.description: Retrieval-augmented generation fails quietly. Here is how to engineer retrieval, grounding, citation checks, and abstention so wrong answers become honest refusals.

item.title: How to Route Intents with Confidence: The Hybrid Classifier Pattern
item.description: Why a single model should never decide everything, and how to build a confidence-gated cascade of rules, a small classifier, and an LLM fallback with self-correcting labels.

item.title: Why Your LLM Judge Is Biased (and How to Audit It)
item.description: LLM-as-a-judge is the cheapest evaluator you will ever have and the easiest to fool. A practical audit protocol for position bias, verbosity bias, self-preference, and agreement with humans.

item.title: How to Put Guardrails on an AI Agent Without Killing It
item.description: Agents fail by doing things, not by saying things. A layered defense of allow-lists, budgets, approvals, and audit trails, plus a red-team loop that proves the guardrails hold.

item.title: How Semantic Caching Cuts LLM Cost, and Why It Can Serve Wrong Answers
item.description: The economics of LLM caching, exact vs. semantic hits, threshold tuning, invalidation, and the subtle ways a cache can return a confidently wrong answer to a different question.

item.title: How to Ship a Model Safely: Shadow, Canary, and the Rollback Button
item.description: Offline metrics do not predict production. A deployment ladder of shadow traffic, canaries with guardrail metrics, and automatic rollback, the SRE way.

item.title: Why Your Training Data Is the Real Model: Curating Data for Small LMs
item.description: Architecture is a commodity; data is the moat. How to find noisy, ambiguous, and memorized examples using the model's own training dynamics, and fix them.

item.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications: A Map of System Trade-offs
item.description: A public-materials review of Martin Kleppmann's 2017 first edition, focused on its data-system concepts, practical boundaries, and relevance to modern ML infrastructure.

item.title: AI Engineering: A Public-Materials Review of Building with Foundation Models
item.description: An evidence-conscious review of Chip Huyen's guide to foundation-model applications, evaluating its documented coverage of evaluation, prompting, retrieval, agents, adaptation, and inference.

item.title: Designing Machine Learning Systems: A Review of the System Around the Model
item.description: An evidence-conscious review of Chip Huyen's 2022 book on the iterative work of building and maintaining machine-learning systems, from data and development to deployment and monitoring.

item.title: Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch): Learning Through Implementation
item.description: An evidence-conscious review of Sebastian Raschka's PyTorch-oriented path through tokenizer construction, GPT architecture, pretraining, and fine-tuning.

item.title: Hands-On Large Language Models: Visualizing the Application Landscape
item.description: A public-materials review of Jay Alammar and Maarten Grootendorst's illustrated, code-oriented tour through embeddings, classification, clustering, search, and generative models.

item.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow: The Psychology Book Every AI Engineer Should Read
item.description: Kahneman's dual-process theory gave AI its favorite metaphor for reasoning models, and it is an even better manual for the biases in your evals, your labels, and your launch decisions.

item.title: Deep Learning by Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville: Still the Foundation
item.description: The canonical deep learning textbook predates transformers, yet its treatment of optimization, regularization, and representation learning explains why modern models work.

item.title: Machine Learning Design Patterns: A Shared Vocabulary for ML Engineering
item.description: Lakshmanan, Robinson, and Munn do for ML what the Gang of Four did for software, naming recurring problems and their solutions so teams can design and review ML systems faster.

item.title: AI Agents in Action: A Practical Tour of Building Autonomous Systems
item.description: Micheal Lanham's hands-on guide covers agent architectures, tool use, memory, planning, multi-agent setups, and evaluation. Here is what it gets right and where production engineers need more.

item.title: Reliable Machine Learning: What Happens When SREs Run Your Models
item.description: Written by Google-veteran SREs and ML practitioners, this book applies Site Reliability Engineering to ML. SLOs, incident response, and organizational design for models in production.
